Darius Bell

gap-022 · supplement · fictional age 16

Written life first, then interpreted by a separate response author without the engine or results. These are synthetic checks. There is no correct career answer key.

Life from age 4 to 16

I don't talk a lot in class because somebody usually answers before I'm ready. At home I talk plenty. I like checking something again and finding out if it's really different or if it just looked different yesterday. People hear fish and think I want a giant tank or a fish business. I mostly like the one I have. I haven't thought that far ahead.

  • family: Lives with his father, an aunt, and two cousins; mother died when he was three, and family speaks about her openly without making every milestone about the loss.
  • finances: Stable lower-middle-income household; adults share expenses and plan large purchases.
  • geography: Beaumont, Texas; several relatives live within a short drive.
  • cultureLanguages: Black American; English at home; family fishing trips and church meals provide regular social contact.
  • school: Public high school; generally solid grades, quiet participation, strong engagement in one laboratory elective.
  • accessOpportunities: School laboratory facilities, a community aquarium group, library resources, and adult support for inexpensive projects.
  • Age 4–5

    Darius spent preschool afternoons at his aunt's kitchen table drawing loops while older cousins did homework. He liked the hum of her aquarium filter and watched the fish longer than anyone expected. His father answered questions about his mother when they arose. Most days were ordinary: snacks, arguments over television, and someone reminding him to put his shoes away.

  • Age 6–7

    He entered school quietly and was sometimes overlooked when louder classmates volunteered. He liked counting objects and explaining rules to one friend at a time. Reading aloud made him tense even when he knew the passage. At home he helped feed the fish with close supervision because his aunt had explained that extra food could make the tank worse.

  • Age 8–9

    At eight he received a small secondhand tank and spent more time choosing stones than researching equipment. His aunt insisted they learn the basics before adding fish. He found the waiting frustrating. Once the tank was established, he kept the same simple routine for months, checking it after school before watching television or playing a familiar racing game.

  • Age 10–11

    A tank developed cloudy water, and Darius and his aunt compared several possible causes using library information and a basic test kit. Some readings confused them. They asked a local aquarium-group member rather than guessing repeatedly. Darius enjoyed keeping numbers in a notebook, although he sometimes wrote only that the water looked fine when he was impatient to do something else.

  • Age 12–13

    In middle school he grew taller quickly and became embarrassed when adults repeatedly suggested basketball. He did not enjoy playing and disliked disappointing them. His closest friend moved across town, so they maintained a quiet friendship through games and occasional visits. Darius found a new lunch seat eventually, but did not feel a need to become part of a large group.

  • Age 14–15

    A school laboratory elective introduced him to pH measurements and comparisons among water samples. Familiarity with his tank helped him ask specific questions without making him good at every science task. He struggled to use the microscope at first and disliked being rushed by a partner. His teacher noticed his orderly notes and asked him to demonstrate a measurement routine privately.

  • Age 16

    At sixteen Darius still maintains the aquarium and is helping compare school tap-water samples collected at different times using approved classroom methods. He likes repeated measurement and modest questions with checkable results. He has never designed a large investigation alone. His father encourages further education without naming a profession. Darius worries that being quiet will make people think he has nothing to contribute.

Life now

  • enjoys: Aquarium care · Repeated measurements · Racing games · Small family fishing outings
  • avoids: Basketball expectations · Fast competitive classroom demonstrations · Large introductions
  • activities: Daily tank maintenance · Laboratory elective · Occasional aquarium-group meetings with his aunt
  • demonstratedSkills: Maintains a long-term care routine · Keeps legible measurement records · Recognizes changes from a familiar baseline · Asks for clarification before changing procedures
  • unfamiliarActivities: Designing complex studies independently · Public presentations · Paid work · Technical programming
  • motivations: Keeping living things healthy · Understanding a specific change · Being trusted without being put on display
  • ambitions: Wants to continue learning about water and living systems · Has not chosen a future role or institution
  • struggles: Low confidence speaking to groups · Assumptions based on height · Impatience when others rush careful work
  • supports: Father and aunt · Observant laboratory teacher · Longstanding friend
  • practicalConstraints: Equipment purchases require budgeting · Rides depend on adult availability · Limited access to advanced facilities

Still uncertain: Will he enjoy broader scientific questions beyond his aquarium context? · What settings allow him to demonstrate knowledge without rushing? · Does he want a larger social role or simply recognition of his current contributions?
